categories.label: Price
categories.purpose: Read the raw traded price, the individual bar’s own open, high, low and close, its price sources (HL2, HLC3, OHLC4), and what the bar did: its candle shape, whether it gapped from the bar before, and how many bars ran one way.
whenToUse: Show the level a decision is being made at.
Reference a bar’s own extremes rather than a derived deviation.
Gate on a candle pattern, a gap or a run of closes as a first-class condition.
bestPractices: Use the last traded price for the live level and a bar fact for what the bar did.
Read the bar state when a provisional bar would change the interpretation.
A pattern carries no trend context: pair it with a trend clause, and hold it within N closes to read "in the last N bars".
commonMisuses: Treating the perpetual mark as the traded price — they are separate metrics.
Comparing raw price levels across assets instead of a percentage relation.
Reading a run length as a gate where a held clause says "N in a row" directly.

examples.title: Last price
examples.description: Read the live traded price, independent of any candle rung.

categories.label: Momentum
categories.purpose: Describe directional impulse, exhaustion, and the pace of price movement.
whenToUse: Confirm whether a move has participation.
Identify overextended or diverging momentum.
bestPractices: Pair level readings with trajectories.
Interpret oscillator extremes in market context.
commonMisuses: Treating an overbought reading as an automatic short.
Stacking several correlated oscillators as independent evidence.

examples.title: RSI trajectory
examples.description: Track the recent RSI build-up and direction.

categories.label: Trend
categories.purpose: Describe direction, persistence, and price location relative to trend references — the moving averages, and the trailing stops (Supertrend, Parabolic SAR) that follow a trend from behind.
whenToUse: Confirm directional structure.
Measure price extension from a moving reference.
Hold a position while price stays on the trend side of a trailing stop.
bestPractices: Use slower references for regime context and faster references for timing.
Read distance together with direction.
Read a trailing stop with its direction: the stop is a level, the direction says which side of it price holds.
commonMisuses: Assuming a lagging average predicts a reversal.
Comparing trend levels without matching timeframes.
Treating a trailing stop as support or resistance it has not been tested at — it moves only with the trend.

examples.title: Distance from SMA 20
examples.description: Measure signed price extension from the 20-period simple moving average.

categories.label: Volatility
categories.purpose: Describe the magnitude and expansion or contraction of market movement.
whenToUse: Calibrate risk to current movement.
Identify squeeze or expansion conditions.
bestPractices: Separate movement size from direction.
Compare volatility on the same timeframe as the decision.
commonMisuses: Reading high volatility as inherently bullish or bearish.
Using raw price-unit volatility across unlike assets.

examples.title: Current ATR
examples.description: Read the latest average true range on the strategy timeframe.

categories.label: Bands & Channels
categories.purpose: Describe the envelope around price — Bollinger, Keltner and Donchian channels — its edges, and where price sits inside it.
whenToUse: Spot price stretched beyond its usual envelope.
Trade a breakout through a channel edge.
Measure room left to the opposite edge.
bestPractices: Read where price sits in the envelope (%B) rather than the raw edge when comparing coins.
Confirm a break of an edge with volume or a close beyond it.
commonMisuses: Treating a touch of the upper band as a sell signal by itself — price walks the band in a trend.
Comparing a band width across assets in price units rather than as a share of price.

examples.title: Riding the upper Bollinger band
examples.description: Hold the close at or just beyond the upper band: %B between 0.8 and 1.2.

categories.label: Volume & Flow
categories.purpose: Describe participation and the balance of buying and selling pressure.
whenToUse: Confirm whether price movement has participation.
Spot flow divergence from price.
Set an absolute activity floor, which needs the raw quantity rather than a ratio.
bestPractices: Use ratios when comparing activity across assets.
Treat flow as confirmation rather than a standalone direction.
Use the raw quantity for a single-coin read or a threshold, and the ratio for a cohort column.
commonMisuses: Equating high volume with bullish demand.
Comparing raw volume counts across structurally different markets.
Comparing raw base-unit volume across assets — that compares denominations, not activity (44,723 BTC beside 2,100,000 DOGE); use the ratio for cohort columns.
Reading a raw per-bar quantity off the forming bar, whose volume ramps from zero each interval — a closed-bar trajectory is the honest read.

examples.title: Volume participation
examples.description: Read current volume relative to its baseline.

categories.label: Derivatives
categories.purpose: Describe positioning, leverage demand, and funding pressure in perpetual markets.
whenToUse: Assess crowded positioning.
Confirm whether exposure is entering or leaving the market.
bestPractices: Combine funding with open-interest change.
Use windowed context for noisy periodic rates.
commonMisuses: Treating positive funding as an immediate short signal.
Interpreting open-interest growth without price context.

examples.title: Funding mean
examples.description: Average the canonical funding history window.

categories.label: VWAP & Profile
categories.purpose: Describe where volume traded — the anchored VWAPs and their standard-deviation bands, the TPO and volume profiles, their value areas and points of control.
whenToUse: Plan entries around the session or anchored VWAP.
Judge whether price trades inside or outside the value area.
Find a naked point of control price has not revisited.
bestPractices: Choose the anchor that matches the holding period: the UTC day for intraday, the week or month for swings.
Read distance from VWAP in percent so coins compare.
commonMisuses: Treating VWAP as a fixed support level when its anchor resets.
Reading a developing profile’s value area as settled before its session closes.

examples.title: Price within ±2% of VWAP
examples.description: Hold price within two percent of the session VWAP, on either side.

categories.label: Sessions & Levels
categories.purpose: Describe the fixed prices a period or a session left behind — the trading sessions’ highs, lows and opens, the opening ranges, the initial-balance extensions, the prior day’s, week’s and month’s highs and lows, and the floor pivots.
whenToUse: Plan entries around the prior day’s high or low.
Trade the break or the sweep of a session’s range.
Use the pivots as targets and stops.
bestPractices: Read a level as a distance in percent so coins compare.
Pair a level with how price reached it — a sweep and a break are different reads.
commonMisuses: Treating every pivot as equally strong.
Reading a session’s high before the session has closed as its final high.

examples.title: Within ±0.5% of the prior day’s high
examples.description: Hold price within half a percent of the previous UTC day’s high, on either side.

categories.label: Market Structure
categories.purpose: Describe the swings price has made, the structure breaks between them, and the active support and resistance zones.
whenToUse: Plan entries around active support or resistance zones.
Measure room to the nearest zone.
Confirm a trend by its higher highs and lows, or a reversal by a break of structure.
bestPractices: Select the side relevant to the proposed direction.
Use structure with momentum or flow confirmation.
commonMisuses: Treating every swing as an equally strong level.
Reading a zone column as the decision timeframe’s levels when its timeframe reference names another rung — a zone column reads zones on its own resolved timeframe.

examples.title: Approaching support
examples.description: Measure signed distance to the nearest active support zone’s top, 0 inside it, held at most 1.5% above it.

categories.label: Regime
categories.purpose: Describe the platform-classified trend, volatility, and momentum environment, the composite regime it resolves to, and the quantities the classifier read to decide.
whenToUse: Adapt tactics to the current market state.
Check whether conditions are changing across observations.
Judge how close a regime is to flipping before sizing against it.
bestPractices: Use regime as context for other evidence.
Review trajectories when transition risk matters.
Read the trend gate before the trend label: a held label is the previous bar’s, carried by the hysteresis buffer rather than re-confirmed by this bar.
Read the margin for how much room the current label has, and both volatility ratios for which of the two inputs is holding it — they must agree, so either alone can be a bar from changing it.
commonMisuses: Treating a regime label as a guaranteed trade direction.
Reconstructing regime labels from unrelated client heuristics.
Reading conviction as how comfortably the regime matched. It encodes WHICH rule in the priority ladder matched — the margins carry comfort.
Treating a trend direction as confirmed without checking whether it came from the decisive DI spread or from the fallback that fires when the spread is indecisive.

examples.title: Trend-regime trajectory
examples.description: Show the recent canonical trend-regime sequence.

examples.title: Distance to a trend flip
examples.description: Read how many ADX points the current trend label survives by — small means a flip is near.

categories.label: Crowd
categories.purpose: Describe aggregate player positioning, confidence, and historical accuracy.
whenToUse: Compare market evidence with participant consensus.
Identify crowded or contrarian conditions.
bestPractices: Treat crowd measures as contextual evidence.
Distinguish popularity from demonstrated accuracy.
commonMisuses: Assuming consensus is always correct.
Using crowd values as candle-timeframe indicators.

examples.title: Crowd pick rate
examples.description: Read the current platform-wide pick rate.

categories.label: Derived
categories.purpose: Describe platform-owned cross-family classifications and convergence facts.
whenToUse: Summarize agreement across canonical evidence families.
Expose platform truth-table outcomes directly.
bestPractices: Use the derived label as a summary and retain its underlying context.
Read the declared vocabulary exactly.
commonMisuses: Recomputing the classification with client-local rules.
Treating a summary label as proof that every input agrees.

examples.title: Flow alignment
examples.description: Read the canonical price-and-flow alignment classification.

categories.label: Market
categories.purpose: Read the whole field at one breadth scope — how much of it closed up or down, carries momentum, participates, is extended, and trades above its own trend — on a section bound to the market at that scope.
whenToUse: Gate an entry on the field not fighting it: a long when the scope is broadly green, a short when it is broadly red.
Read the field’s persistent trend state, which holds for runs of bars, as a risk-on or risk-off label.
Compare two scopes — crypto against TradFi, Layer 1 against memes — with one market section each.
bestPractices: Read the share above EMA 50 for the field’s state, and net breadth for this bar’s move: net breadth flips almost every bar, the trend share does not.
Pin a market column to a timeframe when the strategy should read breadth at another one than its own.
Read the universe beside a share where a small scope makes one coin a large step.
commonMisuses: Treating one bar’s net breadth as a regime — it carries almost no persistence.
Adding a market metric to a coin section — the market is its own subject, bound in the section dialog.
Expecting history before the breadth history began: a lookback before it reads absent.

examples.title: Share above EMA 50
examples.description: Hold the field’s trend state between the risk-off and risk-on lines.
